tooley.q: A Level C software classification is one in which a failure could result in:
opts: fatal injuries to passengers or crew
minor injuries to passengers or crew
aircraft loss
tooley.explain: Table 13.1: level C is a major failure: workload impairs crew efficiency, occupant discomfort including injuries. Aircraft loss is level A; serious or fatal injury is level B.
tooley.detail:
Table 13.1: level C is a major failure: workload impairs crew efficiency and occupants suffer discomfort including minor injuries. Aircraft loss belongs to level A (catastrophic) and serious or fatal injury to level B (hazardous).

Scale: A catastrophic, B hazardous, C major, D minor, E no effect.

tooley.q: A Level B software classification is one in which the probability of failure is:
opts: extremely remote
remote
extremely improbable
tooley.explain: Table 13.1: A is extremely improbable (below 10⁻⁹), B is extremely remote (10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁷), C is remote (10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁵).
tooley.detail:
Table 13.1: A is extremely improbable (below 10⁻⁹), B is extremely remote (10⁻⁹ to 10⁻⁷), C is remote (10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁵), D is probable (above 10⁻⁵). The more severe, the smaller the allowed probability.

Three descriptors: improbable < remote < probable in likelihood.

tooley.q: A software configuration management plan must be created and maintained by:
opts: the CAA or FAA
the aircraft operator
the relevant DO
tooley.explain: Tooley 13.2: the CMP must be devised and maintained by the relevant DO and be effective throughout the life of the equipment.
tooley.detail:
Tooley 13.2: the software configuration management plan (CMP) is devised and maintained by the relevant design organisation (DO) throughout the life of the equipment. The aviation authority (CAA, FAA) approves rather than writes it, and the operator is not responsible for design.

The DO must show the software meets DO-178B/ED-12B.

tooley.q: Weather radar is an example of:
opts: Class B software
Class C software
Class D software
tooley.explain: Table 13.2: level D includes AHRS automatic levelling, CMC/CFDIU, data loader and weather radar.
tooley.detail:
Table 13.2: level D includes AHRS automatic levelling, CMC/CFDIU, data loader and weather radar. Level B includes TCAS, ADS-B transponder and flight displays; level C includes DME and VHF voice.

Intuition: losing weather radar still allows flight, so a low level.

tooley.q: Electronic engine control software is an example of:
opts: LSAP
DFLD
OSS
tooley.explain: The EEC is a typical LSAP target (with DFDAU, APU ECU, FGC). DFLD is data; OSS is typical of IMA units.
tooley.detail:
The EEC (or FADEC) is a typical LSAP target, with the DFDAU, APU ECU and flight guidance computers (FGC). DFLD is field loadable data (FMC and TAWS databases) and OSS is typical of IMA units.

Memory aid: the EEC runs executable code needed for airworthiness, so it is an aircraft part.

tooley.q: OSS and UMS are specific classes of:
opts: DFLD
LSAP
FLS
tooley.explain: FLS (field loadable software) has three types: LSAP, UMS and OSS.
tooley.detail:
FLS (field loadable software) has three types: LSAP, UMS and OSS. DFLD is data, not executable code, so it is a different category.

Diagram: FLS ⊃ {LSAP, UMS, OSS}; DFLD stands apart.

tooley.q: The final stage of loading EEC software is:
opts: verifying the loaded software
switching on and testing the system
disconnecting the PDL
tooley.explain: After removing the loader and reconnecting the cables, run the memory verification program (PASS for part number and checksums), then mark the plate (steps 9 and 10).
tooley.detail:
After removing the loader and reconnecting the cables, run the memory verification program: PASS for the EEC part number and checksums means it was loaded correctly; then write the version, Service Bulletin number and date on the metal plate. Removing the PDL happens before the verification step, and "LOAD COMPLETE" only says the transfer finished.

Lesson: loaded is not the same as correct; verify.

floyd.q: With the BCD code 0111 and EVEN parity, the parity bit is:
opts: Undetermined
floyd.explain: 0111 has three 1s (odd), so the even parity bit must be 1 to make four (even). Matches Table 2-8 (P = 1 for 0111).
floyd.detail:
0111 has three 1s (odd). To make the total even the even-parity bit must be 1, exactly Floyd Table 2-8 (P = 1 for 0111). Setting 0 would leave three 1s, violating even parity.

Quick formula: even parity bit = XOR of the data bits.

floyd.q: What can a parity bit detect?
opts: Any error whatsoever occurring in the group
A single bit error (or an odd number of errors) in the group
Two bit errors within the same group
floyd.explain: Floyd: parity detects a single bit error (or any odd number of errors) but cannot check for two errors in one group.
floyd.detail:
Parity detects a single bit error or any odd number of errors because each error flips the parity. Two errors in one group flip it twice so the parity is unchanged and goes undetected. It also does not say which bit is wrong.

This limit explains why AFDX uses a CRC instead of parity.

floyd.q: In Floyd's CRC example with D = 11010011 and G = 1010, the transmitted code is:
floyd.explain: Append four zeros, divide modulo-2 by 1010 to get remainder 0100; replacing the four zeros with 0100 gives 110100110100. Dividing again by 1010 leaves 0 (checked in code in the notebook).
floyd.detail:
Appending four zeros to 11010011 gives 110100110000; dividing modulo-2 by 1010 gives remainder 0100; replacing the four zeros with 0100 gives the transmitted code 110100110100. Dividing again by 1010 leaves 0. 110100110000 is the data before the remainder is attached.

Verified in the Module 07 notebook.

floyd.q: The receiver divides the received data by the generator code G and finds a NON-ZERO remainder. This means:
opts: Append zeros and divide once more
There is no error, the data is accepted
A transmission error is detected, request retransmission
floyd.explain: Step 7 of Floyd's CRC process: a non-zero remainder means an error has been detected and the receiver requests retransmission.
floyd.detail:
Step 7 of the CRC process: a non-zero remainder means an error is detected (remainder 0100 in Example 2-42) and the receiver requests retransmission. A zero remainder means no error detected. There is no need to append zeros and divide again: the receiver divides once.

Note: in rare cases multiple errors cancel so the remainder is still 0.

floyd.q: According to Floyd, how is the checksum in the ROM test example produced?
opts: Summing each column of bits and discarding carries (XOR of each column)
Dividing the ROM contents by a fixed generator code
Multiplying all the words and keeping the low 8 bits
floyd.explain: Floyd 11-11: the checksum is the sum of each column of data bits discarding the carries, i.e. the XOR sum of each column (Figure 11-74).
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.11 · section 11-11, ROM checksum test
floyd.detail:
Floyd 11-11: the checksum in the ROM example is the sum of each column of bits discarding carries, i.e. the XOR sum by column (Figure 11-74). Multiplying words or dividing by a generator is not how this checksum is made (division belongs to CRC).

A column XOR catches a single-bit error; two errors in the same column may cancel.

floyd.q: Which odd-parity code is in error? (a) 1011 (b) 1110 (c) 0101 (d) 1000
floyd.explain: Odd parity: the number of 1s must be odd; 0101 has two 1s (even) so it is in error.
floyd.detail:
Counting 1s: 1011 has three, 1110 has three, 1000 has one (all odd, valid); 0101 has two (even) so it violates odd parity. Checked in the Module 07 notebook.

Quick test: XOR the bits; a result of 1 means an odd count of 1s.

floyd.q: Which even-parity code is in error? (a) 11000110 (b) 00101000 (c) 10101010 (d) 11111011
floyd.detail:
11000110 has four, 00101000 has two, 10101010 has four (all even, valid). Only 11111011 has an odd count of 1s. Parity only detects the error, does not correct it, and does not say which bit is wrong.

Checked in code.

floyd.q: Add an even parity bit to the end of the code 1010100 (three 1s). The resulting code is:
floyd.explain: Three 1s is odd so the even parity bit is 1: 10101001.
floyd.detail:
To make the count of 1s even, add a 1 to a code with an odd count. The other parts of the problem: 0100000 → 01000001, 1110111 → 11101110, 1000110 → 10001101 (checked). The option with a 0 bit keeps three 1s so it stays odd; the third puts the bit at the front instead of the end.

Putting the parity bit first or last is a system design choice.

floyd.q: In Floyd's modulo-2 operation, what is 1 + 1?
opts: 0 (carry discarded)
floyd.explain: Modulo-2 is binary addition with the carry discarded, which is the XOR gate (Table 2-9).
floyd.src: Floyd Ch.2 · Section 2-12 Checkup #5 and Table 2-9
floyd.detail:
Table 2-9: 00 → 0, 01 → 1, 10 → 1, 11 → 0. Ordinary binary addition gives 1 + 1 = 10 (with carry) but modulo-2 discards the carry leaving 0. Simple rule: the output is 1 if the two bits differ. This is the operation used in CRC division.

Modulo-2 subtraction is identical to modulo-2 addition.

floyd.q: In Floyd Example 2-42 the received data is 100100110100 (one bit in error) with generator G = 1010. The remainder of the division is:
opts: 0100 (non-zero, error detected)
0000 (no error)
floyd.explain: Dividing modulo-2 by 1010 gives remainder 0100, non-zero.
floyd.detail:
The correct transmitted code is 110100110100; the second bit from the left was flipped (1 to 0) giving 100100110100. A non-zero remainder means the receiver detects the error and requests retransmission. If two errors cancel the remainder could be 0 (rare).

Recomputed in the notebook.

floyd.q: The Hamming code is used to detect and correct a single-bit error in a transmitted code.
opts: True
False
floyd.detail: The Hamming code introduces four redundancy bits into a 7-bit group of data bits, at positions 2ⁿ (n = 0, 1, 2, 3). Unlike parity (detect only) and CRC (detect), Hamming also locates the bad bit so it can be corrected. Floyd says the classic version is on the book's website.

floyd.q: According to Floyd the CRC is based on polynomial division using modulo-2 operations.
opts: False
True
floyd.detail: The sender appends zeros to the data, divides by the generator and replaces the zeros with the remainder; the receiver divides again and a zero remainder means no error detected. Floyd's chapter and Tooley 13.4 describe the same idea of attaching a remainder for checking.

floyd.q: A parity bit can detect two bit errors in the same group.
opts: True
False
floyd.explain: False: parity detects a single error (or an odd number of errors).
floyd.detail: Two errors flip the parity twice so it is unchanged. That is why for critical software a CRC is used rather than only parity or a simple checksum (see the demo in Module 07).

generated.q: At which level are flight control and navigation software certified, and why?
opts: Level A, because failure may cause multiple fatalities and loss of the aircraft
Level C, because failure would only make passengers uncomfortable and not affect the flight
Level E, because the pilots can always take over and fly by hand without any automation
generated.explain: Lecture, question 13-3: flight control and navigation are flight critical and so need Level A.
generated.detail:
Lecture 13-3: flight control and navigation are flight critical and so need Level A certification because failure may cause multiple fatalities and loss of the aircraft. Levels C and E match much milder consequences (passenger discomfort or no effect).

Tooley Table 13.2 puts AHRS, GPS/ILS, VOR at level A.

generated.q: What is ARINC 653?
opts: The BPRZ encoding standard ARINC 429 uses to recover the clock from the data signal itself
A specification for space and time partitioning in a real-time operating system, used in IMA
A one-way 100 kbps serial bus standard used for basic avionics in the electronics bay
generated.explain: ARINC 653 lets one processor host applications of different levels without affecting each other; it is not the ARINC 429 bus of Module 05.
generated.detail:
ARINC 653 is the specification for space and time partitioning in a real-time operating system so one processor can host applications of different levels (used in IMA) without affecting each other. It is not a 100 kbps bus (that is ARINC 429) and not the BPRZ code.

Tell ARINC 429 (bus) from ARINC 653 (software).

generated.q: Which standard replaced DO-178B in 2011?
opts: DO-178C
generated.explain: DO-178C was developed in 2011; DO-254 is hardware, DO-160 is environment.
generated.detail:
DO-178C was developed in 2011 to replace DO-178B; DO-254 is the airborne electronic hardware standard and DO-160 the environmental test standard. In July 2013 the FAA issued AC 20-115C recognising DO-178C.

Dates: 1992 (178B), 2011 (178C), 2013 (AC 20-115C).

opts: Low-level requirements to source code, and high-level requirements to test cases
System to high-level requirements, and test cases to test procedures
Software architecture to high-level requirements, and source code to executable object code

The printed answer to question 13-6 names only the second so it is incomplete. See the module's warning box.

generated.q: Which software level needs NO traceability under DO-178C?
opts: Level E
Level C
Level D
generated.explain: Level E needs no traceability because it is non-critical.
generated.detail:
Level E (no effect) needs no traceability because it is non-critical. Level D still needs the green traces and level C needs purple and green.

Trace sets decrease: A (red, purple, green), B and C (purple, green), D (green), E (none).

generated.q: An FLS upgrade may have been corrupted during transfer. What should be done?
opts: Try loading it once to see whether the software runs normally before deciding
Load it and rely only on the LOAD COMPLETE message to conclude it is good
Quarantine it and hold it pending the supplier's integrity or version checks
generated.explain: Tooley 13.3, Key Point box and Test 13.6: if in doubt do not attempt the transfer, quarantine it.
generated.detail:
Tooley 13.3 (Key Point and TYU 13.6): if there is any doubt about the status of an FLS upgrade, do not attempt to transfer it; quarantine it and hold it pending the integrity or version checks specified by the supplier. Trial loading or trusting LOAD COMPLETE is risky because corrupt data can cause erratic operation.

Rule: when in doubt, stop.

generated.q: Which release document usually accompanies a navigation database DFLD?
opts: An EASA Form 1 or FAA 8130-3 as for an LSAP
Only an ordinary Certificate of Conformity
Letter of Acceptance or an equivalent
generated.explain: Tooley 13.3.3: an EASA Form 1 or FAA 8130-3 cannot be provided for navigation database DFLD, so a Letter of Acceptance is used.
generated.detail:
Tooley 13.3.3: an EASA Form 1 or FAA 8130-3 cannot be provided for navigation database DFLD, so a Letter of Acceptance or equivalent accompanies it. Other LSAP and DFLD meeting airworthiness requirements carry a Form 1 or 8130-3; FLS/DFLD without a specific requirement normally need only a Certificate of Conformity.

The module's slide has a table of the three documents.

generated.q: A file has 5 bytes 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. The 8-bit checksum (sum mod 256) is:
generated.explain: 10+20+30+40+50 = 150, below 256 so no wrap-around.
generated.detail:
10 + 20 + 30 + 40 + 50 = 150, below 256 so mod 256 is still 150. 44 is a wrong result (for example 150 + 150 mod 256) and 100 is the sum of the first three numbers.

8-bit checksum = sum mod 256.

generated.q: Two bytes of a file are swapped. A simple additive checksum will:
opts: always be 0, so the file is reported valid
always change, so the error is always detected
stay the same, so the error is not detected
generated.explain: Addition is commutative so byte order does not affect the sum. A CRC does (Demo 1).
generated.detail:
Addition is commutative, so swapping two bytes leaves the sum unchanged and a simple additive checksum cannot detect it. A CRC treats the file as a polynomial so bit order matters and it does detect it (Demo 1 in Module 07).

This is why a CRC is stronger than a checksum.

generated.q: The LAST step in the EEC loading procedure with a PDL is:
opts: write the software version, Service Bulletin number and date on the metal plate
switch on the 115 V AC (400 Hz) supply to the EEC to start loading
insert the software disk into the PDL drive within 5 minutes
generated.explain: Step 10 of Tooley 13.3.
generated.detail:
Step 10 of the EEC procedure: write the software version, Service Bulletin number and date on the metal plate with a ball-point pen. Inserting the disk into the loader (step 6g) and switching on 115 V AC (step 6c) are early steps of loading.

Order: connect, power, load, remove, verify, mark.

generated.q: Before loading an EEC, the software disk must:
opts: be a different version for the left and right engines
be the correct version and not write-protected
be write-protected
generated.explain: Tooley: the same software version for both engines and the disk must not be write-protected.
generated.detail:
Tooley: use the same software version for both engines and the disk must not be write-protected when loading. A write-protected disk can still be read but the loader needs to write, so it reports an error; different versions on two engines could cause different responses.

Figure 13.5 draws the floppy's write-protect window (it must be closed to write).

generated.q: The lecture lists several kinds of documents required for the software development process. Which of these is one of them?
opts: The aircraft's insurance contract
The airline's flight schedule
The software quality assurance plan
generated.explain: The list includes the airworthiness certification plan, SQA plan, CMP, code standard, design standard, traceability, test cases, configuration records, problem reports, the software accomplishments summary, etc.
generated.detail:
The documents fall into four groups: plans (what to do), standards (how), products (requirements, design, code) and evidence (tests, results, records). An insurance contract and a flight schedule are not part of the software development process.

Lecture question 13-1 asks exactly this.

generated.q: What is DO-178 and why is it important?
opts: A standard for optical fibre on aircraft
A standard for the safety of software in aircraft, setting design assurance levels and used by the FAA and EASA as certification guidance
A standard for the aircraft's 115 V 400 Hz supply
generated.explain: Lecture 13-2.
generated.detail: DO-178 (RTCA) or ED-12 (EUROCAE) sets design assurance levels from a safety assessment and hazard analysis of the effect of failure in each system. It is the de facto standard for safety-critical aviation software. Power supplies and optical fibre belong to other standards (ARINC 636 for the optical network).

generated.q: In which year did the RTCA publish DO-178B, and which body published the equivalent ED-12B?
opts: 1992; EUROCAE
2011; EASA
generated.explain: Lecture: DO-178B was published by RTCA in 1992, ED-12B by EUROCAE.
generated.detail: FAA and EASA are the authorities that use DO-178B/ED-12B as certification guidance, not its publishers. 2011 is when DO-178C appeared. Note: DO-178B is not a government regulation; the FAA's AC 20-115C (2013) is what recognises DO-178C.

generated.q: Which DO-178C supplement covers software tool qualification?
generated.explain: DO-330 tools, DO-331 models, DO-332 object-oriented, DO-333 formal methods.
generated.detail:
Four supplements accompany DO-178C: DO-330 (tool qualification), DO-331 (model-based development and verification), DO-332 (object-oriented technology), DO-333 (formal methods). Tools such as MATLAB, Simulink and Embedded Coder support model-based development.

Model-based design is the main reason DO-178B had to be replaced.

generated.q: Which statement is right about modifying software after certification for level A, B and C equipment?
opts: It must not be made unless first approved by the DO
The operator may change it provided it is logged
A technician's on-site signature is enough
generated.explain: Tooley 13.2: all software modifications follow the approval procedures of hardware.
generated.detail:
Because software is an aircraft part, any upgrade at levels A, B and C must be approved by the DO, and every modification must be identified and controlled under the CMP. Only UMS (user modifiable software) may be upgraded by the operator within certified constraints.

Tell apart: an LSAP needs formal release, a UMS is different.

generated.q: What is UMS (user modifiable software) and a typical example?
opts: Mandatory formally released engine control software; for example the EEC
Software the certificate holder declares may be modified within certification constraints; for example ACMS, IFE
A navigation database; for example the FMC
generated.explain: Tooley 13.3.1.2.
generated.detail: UMS can usually be upgraded by the operator, design organisation or equipment manufacturer without further review by the licensing authority. Typical target hardware: aircraft condition monitoring systems (ACMS) and in-flight entertainment (IFE). The second option describes an LSAP and the third a DFLD.

generated.q: What is OSS (option selectable software)?
opts: Software newly written by the operator
Software that runs only on the ground
Approved and validated components the operator may activate within boundaries defined by the certificate holder
generated.explain: Tooley 13.3.1.3: example target hardware is IMA units.
generated.detail:
OSS lets the operator switch on or change built-in options that are already approved, not write new code. So its level of control lies between LSAP (formal release) and UMS (modification within limits).

All three are FLS.

generated.q: How must DFLD (database field loadable data) be treated?
opts: Just stored on an office computer
Like LSAP code: its own unique part number and release documentation
As ordinary data needing no records
generated.explain: Invalid or corrupt data can make a good program misbehave.
generated.detail:
Tooley 13.3.2 stresses that the database embedded in the hardware is not itself field loadable; "loading" only writes new data from a file. Because it affects aircraft performance, the DFLD is tracked like an aircraft part. Examples: FMC, TAWS, IMA.

TYU 13.4 asks exactly this.

generated.q: Among the three ways of distributing FLS and DFLD, "electronic transfer" is:
opts: Distribution over a network with no intermediate media
Posting a disk or CD-ROM
Using a laptop, hand-held computer or portable data loader over a serial link or temporary bus connection
generated.explain: Three ways: media distribution, electronic transfer, electronic distribution.
generated.detail:
The second option is media distribution (floppy, PCMCIA card, CD-ROM, OBRM). The third is electronic distribution (no intermediate media), increasingly used because it is fast and avoids physical media prone to data corruption.

Over the internet you need a firewall and accredited virus protection.

generated.q: Which of the following is NOT necessarily recorded in the register the operator must keep?
opts: Who decides an upgrade is needed and authorises it
The price of the flight's fuel contract
The version of the FLS and DFLD currently installed
generated.explain: The register records version, which aircraft, applicable systems, function, where stored, who is responsible, who decides, and copies traceable to the source.
generated.detail: The register's purpose is configuration control and software traceability. Fuel prices are irrelevant. Note the word NOT: an elimination question.

generated.q: An EASA Form 1 or FAA 8130-3 accompanies which of the following?
opts: The navigation database
An LSAP such as an EEC, DFDAU, APU ECU, FGC or IMA unit
Any FLS not required to meet a specific airworthiness requirement
generated.explain: Tooley 13.3.3.
generated.detail: The second option normally needs only a Certificate of Conformity. The third uses a Letter of Acceptance because a Form 1 or 8130-3 cannot be provided. FMC, TAWS and IMA DFLD meeting airworthiness requirements also carry a Form 1 or 8130-3.

generated.q: Before loading the EEC with the PDL, which supplies feed the loader and the EEC?
opts: 5 V DC to both
115 V AC to the loader and 28 V DC to the EEC
28 V DC to the loader and 115 V AC (400 Hz) to the EEC
generated.explain: Tooley 13.3: step 5 (28 V DC to the loader cable) and step 6c (115 V AC 400 Hz to the EEC).
generated.detail:
The loader cable has three connections: brown (+), black (−) and the shield (chassis ground) for the 28 V DC. The EEC takes the aircraft's 115 V 400 Hz AC. The wrong options swap the roles or use a level not in the procedure.

Link to Module 09: 115 V 400 Hz is the aircraft's AC supply.

generated.q: In the EEC loading procedure, the typical load time and the maximum number of attempts if loading fails are:
opts: About 12 to 16 seconds; at most one attempt
About 2 hours; unlimited attempts
About 12 to 16 minutes; at most three attempts
generated.explain: Tooley 13.3, step 6h.
generated.detail:
If the load fails the transfer-fail lamp lights after a few minutes; check the cables, remove power and repeat, but no more than three attempts if the failure recurs. Insert the disk within 5 minutes of switching on.

The three-attempt limit stops endless attempts on a unit that has a problem.

generated.q: The memory verification program shows FAIL because the FADEC/EEC hardware part number does not agree with the software part number. What should be done?
opts: Ignore it since the EEC still runs
Check the FADEC/EEC hardware part number on the nameplate
Reload with any disk
generated.explain: Tooley 13.3, step 9.
generated.detail:
Step 9 says that if the verify shows FAIL because the hardware and software part numbers disagree, make sure the hardware part number on the nameplate is correct. Ignoring the warning or loading any disk goes against traceability. Use PRINTSCREEN to keep a paper copy of the results.

Principle: the right software must match the right hardware.

generated.q: How is the checksum in Tooley 13.4 made?
opts: By multiplying all the bytes together
By adding the values of consecutive bytes or words and appending the result to the file
By dividing blocks of bits by a fixed number and appending the remainder
generated.explain: The second option is the CRC.
generated.detail:
When preparing to load, the sum is recomputed and compared with the stored value; if different the file must not be used. Both checksum and CRC only indicate whether a file is corrupt and neither is completely fool-proof.

Demo 1 in Module 07 shows the checksum cannot see swapped bytes.

generated.q: The software levels of the VOR and of in-flight entertainment (IFE) are respectively:

Level E and Level A
Level C and Level D

TYU 13.5 asks the trio: weather radar, VOR, IFE.

generated.q: Tooley describes the failure consequence of level B software as:

Workload within crew capabilities; some inconvenience
Flight crew cannot perform their tasks; serious or fatal injuries to some occupants

The second option is level A (catastrophic) and the third is level D (minor). Level B application examples: TCAS, ADS-B transponder and flight displays.

Always, because it saves money

Level E
Level C
